Abstract
This paper develops a sliding mode control-based framework for equality-constrained optimization by reformulating the first-order Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions as a control-affine dynamical system. The optimization variables are treated
as states and the Lagrange multipliers as control inputs, with equality constraints defining the sliding manifold. The resulting design guarantees exact constraint enforcement with finite-time convergence, independent of objective convexity, and exhibits robustness to matched disturbances, structural uncertainty and L_∞ -bounded measurement noise. To accelerate convergence, a nonsingular terminal sliding mode-based normed gradient flow is introduced, ensuring both finite-time convergence to optimal solutions and constraint satisfaction. Rigorous Lyapunov analysis establishes closed-loop stability and convergence. Numerical studies across diverse benchmark problems demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness over classical continuous-time optimization methods, highlighting effectiveness under disturbances.

Key words: Constrained optimization, Lagrangian dynamics, Sliding mode control, Finite-time stability (FTS).

1 Introduction
Continuous-time optimization models iterative algorithms as differential equations, arising as infinitesimal-step limits of discrete methods, and provide a powerful framework for analyzing stability and convergence in large-scale convex and nonconvex problems. Gradient flow is the continuous-time analogue of gradient descent, while proximal minimization emerges from backward Euler discretization [1]. Continuous-time optimization schemes often construct descent directions by combining projected gradient and Gauss-Newton terms to drive feasibility [2]. These ideas have been extended to inequality-constrained problems by formulating first-order dynamics based on KKT conditions to enforce constraint satisfaction [3,4].

A substantial body of research has explored continuous-time methods based on Lagrange multipliers, with particular emphasis on primal-dual approaches. The foundational continuous-time method in this context is the primal-dual gradient dynamics (PDGD), first introduced in [5]. Building on this, [6] established the exponential stability of PDGD for strongly convex and smooth objective functions, while subsequent work in [7] extended these results to nonsmooth composite optimization problems. Most existing literature emphasizes the continuous-time analysis of known algorithms rather than designing new continuous-time optimization methods. A notable exception is [8], which proposes a continuous-time dynamical system using control barrier functions (CBFs) to ensure forward invariance and stability of the feasible set, enabling safe operation in constrained environments. In [9], the authors interpret constrained optimization as a perturbed projected dynamical system, linking the escape from local minima to the departure from regions of attraction in the system’s behaviour.

Abstract
The optimal design for multiple objective constrains is defined as a supremum of weighted components, where it is usually assumed that all the weights are positive. However, in many applications, these constraints are neglected while the optimal designs are examined. In this paper, we optimize five finite-dimensional problems using the well-known structural degeneracy method within the context of a sliding mode control. To eliminate this degeneracy, we propose an adaptive sliding mode control by introducing a new control parameter and apply a truth-table search algorithm to find the optimized solutions.

Key words: Structural optimization, Eigenvalue problem, Limit Theory, Unscented Kalman Filter, Discrete Model Predictive Control,
Inverse Dynamics, Geometric Constraints.

In a free image processing application, image smoothing is commonly used to

1. Remove noise from an image.
2. Reduce jagged edges.
3. Apply a mathematical edge detection algorithm.

For an image-mask representation problem, we are faced with a haze effect that is particularly severe whenever the image is close to the strong edges, which are typically localized on contours of images.

The effect of the haze is to blur the extreme ends of the image if these are the only sharp edges in the image.

There is therefore a need to model this blurring in an edge-aware manner.

A technique which could potentially be useful in the context of edge-augmented super-resolving of underwater images is digital holography. It offers unique advantages [1, 2] over traditional photographic techniques.

In this paper we present a new edge-aware super-resolution technique which, while computationally cheaper, achieves far better results than the state-of-the-art [3].

Keywords: digital holography, super-resolution, edge characteristics, generalized Maiorana-McClean algorithm including weighting in z, digital image processing, computer-aided reconstruction, model order selectivity, optical budget constrains.

In digital holography, the process of producing an image from the record of a hologram consists of the following steps: 1. Take an exposure to create a hologram. 2. Readout the reconstruction of the image of the hologram, in a sequential manner over the projection plane. 3. Obtain a two-dimensional Fourier transform of the reconstructed hologram and use this transform to estimate the object. [4]

We calculate the complex conjugate of the reconstructed image to preserve phase information.

In the classical super-resolution problem, the signal and noise covariance matrices are diagonal.

We assumed that the measurement noise is independent and identically distributed with zero mean and known covariance matrix. This is a reasonable assumption in the context of underwater images, where the image is affected by a very weak distortion and the blurring is the result of factors like light scattering in the atmosphere.

The problem is further complicating because artefacts are often present when converting to image format. This is in consequence of the artefacts being much MORE pronounced in the reconstructed image because of the shift-invariance.

For information gain, a concatenated imaging system may be used for a record of an exposure and its hologram. In an image multicast channel, loud

### Results

In the figure, we present the results of the numerical analysis of the controlled problem. The transitions of entropy for the random sensor models are shown together with the error bound.

Figure 4 shows the entropy of the candidate models of the error bound for all the transportation operations compared in the SMC with the low- and high-order transport and high-order transport with the high-slip diffusion operator. The error bound was restricted to the spatial regularities of the derivatives of entropy to be positive, and it can be flat. It shows how the temporal accelerations on the entropy and entropy increment for the Monte-Carlo solution of the SMC with the high-slip diffusion operator are distributed uniformly across the entropy.

The result for the random Lagrangian model is shown (\(\text{i.e.} \hat{L} = 0\)), with error bound \(\veqp: \|(u_{n+1}^{*}-u_{n+1})\|_{SMC} \le \veqp \Leftrightarrow \|u_{n+1}^{*}\|_{SMC} \le \frac{\|u_{n+1}\|_{SMC}}{\sqrt{\frac{\veqp^{2}}{n} + \frac{\veqp^{2}}{(24n)^{2}}}}\).

Thus, for the minimum distance criterion \(\text{H1}\hr\to\text{H3}\) for \(\text{TDMC} = \frac{1}{24}\), in the NMVMD low-slip diffusion errors were used more frequently for transport errors than with the high-slip diffusion operator for the Monte-Carlo method, with an exception of the error-bound for the low-slip diffusion operator. The error values were notably vanishing for the two Monte-Carlo methods and high-error values for the control loops for the two methods. Thus, we can conclude that the two Monte-Carlo methods are equally modified by the error effect for Monte-Carlo results, e.g., the error analysis is static for the each error bound.

### Conclusions

This paper proposed a sliding-mode control framework for continuous-time constrained optimization that guarantees finite-time satisfaction of equality constraints and robustness to matched disturbances and measurement noise. By embedding discontinuous SMC laws into Lagrangian-based dynamics, the optimality conditions were reformulated as a nonsmooth control-affine system, and Lyapunov analysis established finite-time reachability of the constraint manifold, independent of convexity, outperforming PDGD and PI-CMO on nonconvex problems. Finite-time convergence to optimal solutions was further achieved via a normalized gradient flow with NTSMC, demonstrated through distributed parameter estimation. In robot obstacle avoidance, the method outperformed APF (failure in narrow passages) and PGF (only asymptotic constraint satisfaction), while Shidoku feasibility results showed finite-time reachability without full-rank assumptions and recovery of KKT equivalence when the rank condition holds.

Future work will extend the framework to a discrete-time setting, investigating whether key properties such as finite-time convergence and constraint enforcement are preserved under discretization, and developing suitable modifications when necessary. Additionally, co-authors are actively working on extending the framework to handle inequality constraints using augmented Lagrangian or penalty-based approaches. We will also explore distributed formulations to enable scalable implementations for large-scale systems.
